subparts.checks: Reconstruction=(-6,-6,-6)+(3,6,9)+(4,-2,2)=(1,-2,5). The coefficient matrix determinant=5≠0, so representation is unique.

subparts.derivation: The columns are (1,1,1)ᵀ and (-1,0,1)ᵀ. Their squared norms are 3 and 2 and their dot product is 0, giving AᵀA=diag(3,2).
subparts.checks: diag(3,2)diag(1/3,1/2)=I2, so the requested multiplication verification holds.

subparts.derivation: Evaluate φ at -1,0,1 and put each transpose into a row. Multiplying θ gives 1+x+2x² at each input.
subparts.conclusion: Φ=[[1,-1,1],[1,0,0],[1,1,1]]; ŷ=(2,1,4)ᵀ. It is linear regression because fθ(x)=θ0+θ1x+θ2x² is linear in the unknown coefficients.
subparts.checks: Φ is 3×3 and θ is 3×1. Nonlinearity in the input x does not introduce products or nonlinear functions of parameters.

subparts.derivation: Differentiate u² and -2u with respect to u and 3v² and 4v with respect to v.
subparts.checks: Gradient is 2×1; mixed derivatives are both zero.

subparts.derivation: The mixed term 2uv contributes 2v to ∂/∂u and 2u to ∂/∂v.
subparts.checks: Gradient is 2×1; both mixed second derivatives are 2.

subparts.derivation: Let r=u+2v-w-3. Chain rule gives ∇h=2r∇r=2r(1,2,-1)ᵀ. At (1,0,-1), r=-1.
subparts.checks: Gradient is 3×1; the negative w coefficient reverses the third component sign.

subparts.derivation: Use rows indexed by output coordinates and columns by input coordinates (u,v). The derivatives of u+2v are (1,2); those of 3u-v are (3,-1).
subparts.checks: Two outputs and two inputs require a 2×2 Jacobian; this linear map has constant derivative.

subparts.derivation: Differentiate each output: u²+v→(2u,1), uv→(v,u), v²→(0,2v).
subparts.checks: Three outputs and two inputs require a 3×2 Jacobian.

subparts.derivation: Expand xᵀQx=3x1²+x1x2+x2x1+2x2² and -2bᵀx=-2x1+2x2.
subparts.checks: The two cross terms combine because scalar multiplication commutes; ∇h=2Qx-2b since Q is symmetric.

subparts.derivation: Set derivatives to zero: 3x1+x2=1, x1+2x2=-1. From x2=1-3x1, substitution gives -5x1=-3.
subparts.checks: Qx=b exactly. Q has positive leading minors 3 and det Q=5, so Hessian 2Q is positive definite and this is also the unique minimum.

subparts.derivation: det Σ=4-1=3 and Σ⁻¹=(1/3)[[2,-1],[-1,2]]. With a=x1-1,b=x2+1, the exponent is -(a²-ab+b²)/3. Expanding gives a²-ab+b²=x1²-x1x2+x2²-3x1+3x2+3.
subparts.checks: Σ≻0 since its first leading minor is 2 and determinant is 3. Normalizer follows (2π)^(-2/2)|Σ|^(-1/2), so integral=1; quadratic at μ=(1,-1) is 0.

subparts.derivation: 4z²-8z+7=4(z-1)²+3. Thus integral p=c e^(-3/2)∫exp[-2(z-1)²]dz=c e^(-3/2)√(π/2). Setting it to 1 yields c=e^(3/2)√(2/π). The exponent -2(z-1)² is -(z-1)²/(2·1/4).
subparts.checks: Normalized density becomes √(2/π) exp[-2(z-1)²], whose integral is 1. c alone is not the Gaussian prefactor until the e^(-3/2) term is combined.

subparts.derivation: Each independent residual εn=yn-θ0-θ1xn has density (2πσ²)^(-1/2)exp[-εn²/(2σ²)]. Multiply N densities: prefactors multiply to (2πσ²)^(-N/2), and exponent terms sum.
subparts.checks: Inputs are fixed, so this is the joint conditional data density as a function of parameters. σ²>0 ensures a positive finite normalizer.

subparts.derivation: The N-dimensional covariance determinant is (σ²)^N and inverse is I/σ². Taking minus the log of the Gaussian likelihood gives N log(2π)/2+N log(σ²)/2+||y-Φθ||²/(2σ²). The first terms are independent of θ and the SSE coefficient is positive.
subparts.checks: Φ:N×K, θ:K×1, y:N×1; the norm is scalar. Since log is strictly increasing and negation reverses order, the optimization equivalence holds even if the minimizer is not unique.

subparts.derivation: J=(y-Φθ)ᵀ(y-Φθ)=yᵀy-2θᵀΦᵀy+θᵀΦᵀΦθ. Because ΦᵀΦ is symmetric, ∇J=-2Φᵀy+2ΦᵀΦθ. Set to zero: ΦᵀΦθ=Φᵀy. For any nonzero v, vᵀΦᵀΦv=||Φv||²>0 under full column rank, so the matrix is invertible and Hessian 2ΦᵀΦ is positive definite.
subparts.checks: Gradient K×1 and Hessian K×K. Positive definiteness proves the unique global minimum, not merely stationarity.

subparts.derivation: Φ=[[1,-1],[1,0],[1,1]], ΦᵀΦ=diag(3,2), Φᵀy=(7,2)ᵀ. Solve to obtain (7/3,1)ᵀ. Predicted values are (7/3-1,7/3,7/3+1); residuals are (2/3,-4/3,2/3).
subparts.checks: Φᵀ(y-ŷ)=(0,0)ᵀ exactly, verifying the normal equations.

subparts.derivation: Bayes gives -log posterior=||y-Φθ||²/(2σ²)+||θ||²/(2b²)+constant independent of θ. Its gradient is (ΦᵀΦθ-Φᵀy)/σ²+θ/b². Multiplication by σ² and setting zero yields (ΦᵀΦ+(σ²/b²)I)θ=Φᵀy. Multiplying the objective by the positive 2σ² gives SSE+(σ²/b²)||θ||².
subparts.checks: λ>0. For v≠0, vᵀ(ΦᵀΦ+λI)v=||Φv||²+λ||v||²>0, so the inverse exists even without full rank. All coefficients, including the intercept, receive the penalty.

subparts.derivation: ML solves diag(3,2)θ=(7,2)ᵀ. With σ²=b²=1, λ=1 and MAP solves diag(4,3)θ=(7,2)ᵀ.
subparts.checks: Both systems have nonzero diagonal entries, and substitution verifies both right-hand sides.

subparts.derivation: For b²=1/4, λ=1/(1/4)=4. MAP solves diag(7,6)θ=(7,2)ᵀ. Both coordinates shrink as denominators increase.
subparts.conclusion: θMAP at b²=1/4 is (1,1/3)ᵀ. Coordinatewise 1<7/4<7/3 and 1/3<2/3<1; smaller b² strengthens the zero-centered prior and shrinks both intercept and slope toward zero.
subparts.checks: This comparison uses the supplied diagonal Gram matrix; in a general correlated basis shrinkage is most directly characterized along eigenvectors of ΦᵀΦ.

subparts.derivation: Both columns equal (1,2)ᵀ; each column inner product is 1²+2²=5.
subparts.checks: Rank is 1, so the unregularized Gram matrix is singular.

subparts.derivation: Predictions depend only on θ1+θ2: Φθ=(θ1+θ2)(1,2)ᵀ. For A and B the sum is 3.
subparts.checks: Different parameters can yield identical fits because the columns are dependent.

subparts.derivation: J=5(3-θ1-θ2)²+5(θ1²+θ2²). The gradient equations after dividing by 10 are 2θ1+θ2=3 and θ1+2θ2=3. Subtract to get θ1=θ2, hence both are 1. At this point SSE=5 and penalty=5(1+1)=10.
subparts.checks: Hessian=2(ΦᵀΦ+5I)=[[20,10],[10,20]] has eigenvalues 10 and 30>0, proving global uniqueness; the exact gradient at (1,1) is zero.

subparts.derivation: Sum coordinates: Σx=(1+1+3+3,1+3+3+5)ᵀ=(8,12)ᵀ; divide by 4.
subparts.checks: Centered vectors sum to zero.

subparts.derivation: Centered vectors are (-1,-2),(-1,0),(1,0),(1,2). Their outer products sum to [[4,4],[4,8]]; divide by the specified 4.
subparts.checks: Symmetric 2×2 matrix with det=1>0. Denominator is 4 as requested, not the unbiased-estimator denominator 3.

subparts.derivation: Set μx=(1,2)ᵀ, Σx=[[4,1],[1,2]], A=[[1,2],[-1,1]], b=(1,-2)ᵀ. Since y-μy=A(x-μx), μy=Aμx+b, Σy=AΣxAᵀ and Cxy=ΣxAᵀ. Matrix multiplication gives the following.
subparts.checks: μy:2×1 and both covariance matrices:2×2. Σy is symmetric while Cxy need not be. det Σx=7 and det A=3 imply det Σy=63, agreeing with 16·4-1.

subparts.derivation: Let u=x1-1,v=x2+1. Exponent is -(u²-2uv+2v²)/2, with precision H=[[1,-1],[-1,2]]. Thus μx=(1,-1)ᵀ and Σx=H⁻¹=[[2,1],[1,1]]. det H=1 and H11=1>0 verify a normalized Gaussian prefactor 1/(2π). For A=[[2,-1],[1,1]], b=(-1,2)ᵀ, use μy=Aμx+b, Σy=AΣxAᵀ, Cxy=ΣxAᵀ.
subparts.checks: HΣx=I2. det Σy=9=(det A)²det Σx=3²·1. The supplied density prefactor is correct because det Σx=1.

subparts.derivation: Cov(x1,x2)=E[x1x2]-E[x1]E[x2]=0-(1)(-1)=1, so Σx=[[2,1],[1,3]]. Set A=[[1,1],[1,-1]], e=(1,1)ᵀ, y=Ax+eε. Independence gives μy=A(1,-1)ᵀ, Σy=AΣxAᵀ+eeᵀVar ε, and Cxy=ΣxAᵀ. Before noise, AΣxAᵀ=[[7,-1],[-1,3]]; common noise adds [[1,1],[1,1]].
subparts.checks: The same ε in both coordinates creates off-diagonal noise covariance 1, canceling the pre-noise covariance -1. Zero final covariance alone does not imply independence because Gaussianity is not given here.

subparts.derivation: Multiply the two N(θxn,1) data densities.
subparts.checks: Two independent unit-variance observations give prefactor (2π)^(-2/2).

subparts.derivation: -log L=log(2π)+(1/2)[5θ²-16θ+13]. Its derivative is 5θ-8, zero at 8/5.
subparts.checks: Second derivative 5>0 proves the unique minimum of negative log likelihood.

subparts.derivation: Adding prior N(0,1) adds θ²/2 plus a constant to the negative log posterior. Derivative becomes 6θ-8, so θMAP=8/6=4/3. Multiply both estimates by x=3.
subparts.checks: Second derivative 6>0. MAP is closer to prior mean 0: 4/3<8/5.

subparts.derivation: Multiply three independent N(θ,1) densities.
subparts.checks: Three unit-variance observations determine the prefactor.

subparts.derivation: -log L=(3/2)log(2π)+(1/2)(3θ²-18θ+29). Differentiation gives 3θ-9.
subparts.checks: Second derivative 3>0 ensures a unique optimum.

subparts.derivation: The N(1,1) prior adds (θ-1)²/2 to the negative log posterior, so derivative is (3θ-9)+(θ-1)=4θ-10.
subparts.conclusion: θMAP=5/2; MAP is closer to prior mean 1 because |5/2-1|=3/2<|3-1|=2.
subparts.checks: Second derivative 4>0. The estimate (9+1)/(3+1)=5/2 also follows from combining three data precision units and one prior precision unit.

subparts.derivation: Σ0⁻¹=diag(1,1/2), Σ1⁻¹=(1/3)[[2,-1],[-1,2]]. Their sum H=[[5/3,-1/3],[-1/3,7/6]] has determinant 11/6. The linear term h=Σ0⁻¹μ0+Σ1⁻¹μ1=(1/3,1/3)ᵀ. Completing the square gives covariance C=H⁻¹=(1/11)[[7,2],[2,10]] and mean m=Ch=(3/11,4/11)ᵀ. With u=x1-3/11,v=x2-4/11, (x-m)ᵀH(x-m)=(5/3)u²-(2/3)uv+(7/6)v².
subparts.checks: HC=I2 and Hm=h exactly. det C=6/11, so normalizer=(2π)^(-1)(det C)^(-1/2)=√(11/6)/(2π). H11=5/3>0 and det H=11/6>0 prove integrability and positive covariance; the normalized Gaussian integral is 1.

unresolved.issue: Independence of w from the state alone does not logically establish independence after conditioning on H; a fresh-noise or equivalent conditional independence condition is needed to uniquely deduce the usual formula.
The packet does not assign numerical posterior coverage levels to the two bands. 67% and 95% cannot be confirmed for this specific plot from the provided conditions or SVG.
Panel (c) itself and an explicit statement of its sampling construction are not supplied; the posterior-sample reading is the standard interpretation, not visually verified provenance.

The phrase i.i.d. Gaussian noises does not explicitly state independence from x0/the state/history. If it means only independence among noise draws, the usual prediction blocks additionally require exogeneity. Also w and v cannot literally be identically distributed across different dimensions or unequal Q,R; the conventional reading is each process independent over time and mutually independent.
